translation:
_Tirath vrat vakh veladi, rahi choho jug chhaaye. Kabire mool nikandiya, so kaun halahal khaay._ (Pilgrimage and fasting are like a poisonous creeper that has spread and endured through all four ages; Kabir uprooted it entirely -- who, then, would still go on eating that deadly poison?)

Even so, the followers of the Kabir panth (path) keep a fast on the full-moon day (punam), and if there is an eclipse, they observe the fast either a day before or a day after the full moon. Yet in their own account of the glory of the full moon they themselves record that a mother, for her son's sake, once fed a saint even while she herself was in her menstrual state (rajasvala). Kabir opposed ritualism -- fasting, japa, tapa, and vows -- yet by keeping such fasts the followers of the Kabir panth are transgressing Kabir's own principles and, in effect, murdering Kabir himself. There may be a few discerning people, such as Krishnakant Malaviya, but the people of Indian culture, having become slaves to brahminical religious authorities, have grown weak; and it is of no use at all merely to recommend that such religious authorities -- who wish to make the Ganga flow backward -- be restrained from the tyranny they inflict upon society. It was Jivandasji, whose heart ached for the whole of India and indeed the whole world, who, with great courage, removed the taint of the menstrual taboo on the second day of the bright half of Ashadh, in Vikram Samvat 1734. Thus, in the entire world, only a single revolutionary soul was ever born; the mahants of the devotee community, whose own conduct is such that they would rather see a household break apart than change, may well be unable to encourage the devotee community that follows Jivanji's principles -- that would be no great matter -- but let them at least refrain from committing the sin of reintroducing the taint of ritualism. Consider: it was Jivandasji who, with such ease, cast aside ritualism, and gave up and eradicated japa, tapa, yagna, astrology, the fixing of auspicious moments, and the like; and it was that same Maharaj Jivanji who, in order to remove the taints held against women, must have endured anguish right up to his final hour -- and at the very end of his life he removed this taint of menstruation. Thus this revolutionary soul, who had come down to this earth to accomplish this very work, completed this, his final task. In the Samagam, this chapter on the removal of women's taint is reckoned as the last chapter; the chapter on his departure to his eternal abode (swadham) that follows presents the completion of his life's work. By removing the taint of menstruation, Jivanji has, in the whole world, done the work of a truly singular hero -- something that no one has been able to do to this day, and it seems unlikely that anyone will be able to do it in the future either. Let there be millions upon millions of salutations to such a great soul. Blessed is this Jivanji, and blessed too is the Uda devotee community that has kept his principles alive to this day. But as for the mahants who consider themselves great while striving to make others transgress the very principles Jivanji established -- no language can find a fitting title by which to address them.

At Kunvarpura there was once a katha (religious discourse) given by Narhari Maharaj. He had been impressed by our community, but when he learned that, because we do not accept ritualism, we also do not observe the menstrual taboo, he said in his katha, "For devotees such as yourselves to be devotees and yet not observe the rajasvala taboo -- that is wrong." Bhagat Mohanbhai Vrundavan of Kandevar, who was present at the katha, privately said to the Maharaj, "Could it be that Jivanji Maharaj gave us this instruction without understanding it? We, after all, follow our guru's instruction. He must surely have provided some remedy for the rajasvala taboo as well." At this the Maharaj said, "Should any lapse, knowingly or unknowingly, occur in observing the rajasvala taboo, he has already redeemed us for it by instituting the offering of a savapanchsher thali -- a ceremonial plate of a set measure -- on Sama Pancham, in the celebration of the day of his departure to his eternal abode. In this way he has already removed, on our behalf, the taint attached to the rajasvala taboo."

In the Bhaktamal, an episode about a varamukhi (a courtesan) is described. There was a beautiful courtesan of the South, colourful and full of charm, whose outward splendour, too, was fine. One day a company of saints, seeing her magnificent grandeur, stopped there and spread their seats on the ground; images of the Lord (Thakorji) were also set up on their thrones. Seeing them, the courtesan was delighted, and, filling a plate with gold coins, began to offer it to the head of the saints; but he did not accept the courtesan's wealth, and instead instructed her, "Shri Rangji himself will accept your wealth." So she went to offer a crown worth three lakh rupees to Shri Rangji, but just then she entered her menstrual period, and drew back. Yet the Lord bowed His head and showed His readiness to have the crown placed on Him, and so she placed the crown upon the Lord. The Lord is one who shows such fond, doting affection toward His devotees. [unclear] This account appears in an article in "Bhola Pani," Registration No. 2121, page 32; its translation is in Jivanvani, Issue 18, page 19. That this courtesan's name was Chintamani is recorded in Moksha Patrika, Registration No. 239, page 1727. Registration No. 242-4, page 628, also carries the full account of this courtesan.

On the subject of exclusive devotion (ananyata), the revered Yadunath writes, on the back of page 21 of Lintiyu no. 1: "I have purchased a woollen shawl from a Shah, a resident of Dabhoi, in whose name lies my own deliverance." He would say that, being one of the seven sons of Vallabhacharya, he was a follower of the Gokulnath lineage, and that his neck-thread (kanthi) belonged to that lineage. Even if we must go out of the village, our household deity's service is not to be entrusted to anyone else -- the women of our own house perform it, but it is not to be entrusted even to a neighbour. Even if the woman is in her monthly courses, she still performs it.

There was a police officer of Sankheda named Bhat Fojdar, who used to say: "What Khuda (God) does not do, Uda does."

At Jagannath Puri, no pilgrim lights a hearth of his own; only Jagannath's own prasad is eaten -- yet the Uda community has the freedom to prepare their own prasad without such restriction.

Thus the Uda devotee community truly stands apart, distinguished from every other community; yet, on the matter of the rajasvala taboo, the followers of the Pushtimarg, because of their exclusive devotion, have obtained an exemption from the taboo -- which resembles, to some extent, our own practice. Our own womenfolk, however, have never at all accepted the notion of impurity attached to the menstrual state, and so on -- and it is indeed true that our way of life appears to those bound by ritual to be of quite a different kind. The Vaishnavs of the Pushtimarg practise a devotion bound up with the three gunas (trigunas), whereas we practise a devotion that transcends the three gunas altogether. At Shahapura, the sannyasi Maheshvaranandji once told me: "Vaishnavah panchamo varnah" -- Vaishnavas stand apart from all four varnas. Where eighteen kinds of varna are reckoned, we, the Uda devotees, say that ours is the nineteenth varna, and the feeling behind it is that we are distinct from all of them.

Narsinh Mehta has said, in a kirtan (hymn) set to the raga Sindhudo:

_Harinaam vina nar sootki re, mahapaataki re tene aabhadvano adhikar nahi, evi Ved Puraane vaani ja kahi._ (Tek.) (Without the Name of Hari, a man remains in a state of sutak, ritual impurity -- he is a great sinner, and no one has the right even to touch him. Such is the word declared in the Vedas and Puranas.)

Without devotion to God's Name, every human being remains in a state of sutak; therefore no one has any right to touch, that is, to have social dealings with, such a person. Such is the pronouncement made in the Vedas and Puranas. Women are dubbed untouchable when they are in the state of menstruation. The only real point behind this is that, in such a state, sexual intercourse with a woman ought not to take place -- such restraint is what ought to have been observed; but instead of that, women themselves have been made out to be utterly polluted. That women undergo the menstrual state is a natural law, but the scriptures and Puranas have given it the form of stories and legends and thereby made it seem an acceptable rule; the chief reason for this is simply that ordinary people will keep to moral codes of discipline only if they are shown some fear or superstition of this kind.

With this purpose in view, the story of a killing committed by Indra is given in the Bhagavata, Canto 6, Chapters 7-8. The arrogant Indra, on one occasion, did not rise to honour his guru Brihaspati, and so the guru departed from there. Thus, deprived of their guru, the gods' radiance was destroyed; Brihaspati's rival Shukracharya then helped the asuras, the demons, and thereby won heaven for them. The gods, having lost their lustre, then entreated Vishvarupa, the son of Tvashta, asking him to accept the role of guru and become their priest (purohit), but Vishvarupa said that the office of purohit is a very lowly one.

_Pitharhitam dharmashilai brahmavarch-upavyayam._ (The work of a purohit consumes and wastes away one's brahma-tej, spiritual radiance; for this reason, righteous, dharma-minded sages have condemned it.)

Tulsidas has said, in the Ramayana:

_Uparohitya karma ati manda, Bed Puran sumrati kar ninda._ (The work of the priesthood is a very base one; the Vedas, the Puranas, and the Smritis all condemn it.)

_Adhikaari stri-maasau, mathapatyas tribhir dinaih, shidhram narakam avapnoti, dinam ekam purohitah._ (An officiant attains hell in three months, and the head of a monastery in three days; but if one wishes to attain hell most swiftly of all, let him become a family priest for even a single day.)

Despite knowing this, Vishvarupa still accepted the office of guru; and to Indra he gave the Narayana-kavach, a protective mantra-armour of Vaishnava devotion. By virtue of this Vaishnava knowledge, Indra achieved victory over the demons; but at the time of a yajna, Indra grew suspicious of him. Since Vishvarupa was the son of a mother of demon lineage, he would secretly offer oblations to the demons as well, and so Indra cut off all three of his heads. With one mouth he used to drink soma-rasa, with the second mouth he drank liquor, and with the third he ate ordinary food. By slaying him, Indra incurred the sin of brahma-hatya, the killing of a brahmin. Indra bore this sin for a year, and then divided it among four benefactors who each accepted a share on his behalf. The earth accepted a quarter share, and because of this, part of the earth became desert wasteland; Indra then blessed the earth, saying, "Whatever pits and hollows form in you shall, in the course of time, fill up again." The trees accepted a quarter share, and this is why gum forms in them -- as a result of that portion of the killing; and since gum is thus a product of that killing, the Vaishnavs of the Pushtimarg do not eat it. But for the Uda devotee community, there is no objection at all to eating any kind of gum. Indra blessed the trees, saying, "Even when you are cut down, your branches will sprout again." Water accepted a quarter share of the killing, and this is why bubbles form in water; Indra blessed it, saying, "You shall go on increasing" -- and this is why, however much water is drawn from wells and the like, it never runs dry. Women accepted the fourth quarter of the killing, and this is why they must undergo the state of menstruation. In compensation, Indra granted them the boon of being able to enjoy intercourse without restriction.

Prabhudatt Brahmachari writes, in Bhagwati Katha, Part 41, page 40: "The Lord said: women's monthly flow, the bubbles in water, barren wasteland, and the gum of trees -- these four portions of the killing of a brahmin turn out to be of great use as well. Everything is stuck together using gum. Resin and guggul are themselves a form of gum, from which incense is made. Baroza is a gum used to condition the strings of the sarangi. Asafoetida, too, is a gum, and it is used to temper dal, vegetables, and other such foods."

Indra's sin of brahma-hatya was thus removed; but Tvashta, the father of Vritrasura, then brought forth, by means of a mantra, a son named Vritrasura for the very purpose of killing Indra. But in the recitation of the mantra a mispronunciation occurred, so that instead of the mantra bringing about Indra's death, it turned out that Vritrasura would die by Indra's hand -- and so Indra slew Vritrasura. In devotion to Vishnu, even if an error occurs in the pronunciation of the sacred syllables, importance is given to the devotional feeling of the one reciting them; so even if "Mara" is uttered instead of "Rama," it is still counted as the remembrance of Rama alone. It is only worshippers of a tamasic disposition who must be careful about correct pronunciation. Because of this killing, the sin of brahma-hatya again fell upon Indra; but since Vishvarupa had earlier given him the Narayana-kavach, by the power of remembering that Name he escaped from the sin. Indra had committed an offense against the Name, and that offense was removed only through remembrance of the Name. Thus, the fault of an offense against the Name is removed only by remembrance of the Name. So it was that, once again, by the power of the Narayana-kavach, Indra regained the kingdom of heaven. Such is the account. But those bound by ritualism regard the state of menstruation as a defilement, and make efforts to remove the resulting sutak, ritual impurity.

In the Samagam it is clearly stated that a woman (abala, "the powerless one") is bound by the bonds of her husband; her duty is to follow after her husband. Therefore, whatever karma the husband performs, its fault must be borne by the husband himself; the woman does not incur the fault of karma performed by her husband. For women, no new karma is generated. Men, however, must perform many kinds of karma without any such exemption -- charity, meritorious acts, vows, pilgrimage, study, teaching, fire-offerings, the accepting of gifts, circumambulation of the earth, and so on -- countless millions of blows of karma of this kind fall upon ritualistic brahmins, but such karma does not attach to women. Having given this instruction on the removal of karma for women, Jivandasji, overcome with emotion, said: "Father, the Lord of Mercy, cherishes all with fond affection" -- meaning that the merciful Lord showers His grace on everyone without exception; but if souls give up the net of worldly attachment and walk on, then they attain bliss, happiness, and well-being. Eight kinds of karma have been enumerated: 1. Mansa karma (karma of the mind), 2. Netra karma (karma of the eyes), 3. Vacha karma (karma of speech), 4. Hasta-praharan karma (karma of striking with the hands), 5. Dehadik karma (karma of the body), 6. Shravan-dhyan karma (karma of hearing and meditation), 7. Krit karma (karma already performed), 8. Svastha karma (karma of health and well-being).

Of these, mansa karma alone cannot be removed. Karmas arise in many different ways, and there are also three defects: 1. Kayik -- karmas that arise from the body, 2. Vachik -- karmas that arise from speech, from what is spoken, 3. Mansik -- karmas that arise from the mind, from its resolves, 4. Sansargik netra karma -- karmas arising from contact, touch, and the like.

Of the kayik faults there are three: 1. theft, 2. adultery, 3. violence to living beings.
Of the vachik faults there are three: 1. slander, 2. false speech, that is, telling lies, 3. harshness, that is, speaking bitter words to one who is present.
Of the mansik faults there are three: 1. trishna, craving -- entertaining trivial sensual desires, 2. dveshbuddhi -- the tendency to see faults in others, 3. anger.

Mansa karma, the story of the princess.

In all, there are thus nine defects, of mind, speech, and body. If one renounces these, then satsang (holy company) becomes truly fruitful. As an illustration of how mansa karma cannot be removed, there is the story of a certain king's daughter. This daughter lived in an upper mansion built on pillars. Once a courtesan came and lodged there, and to the courtesan's lodging a paramour would come. The king's daughter began watching him, and because of this a bondage formed in her mind. Due to this bond of karma, when she lay sleeping, her maidservant one day saw, in her mouth, marks of play, and on her body flecks of blue dye scattered about. The maidservant reported this to the king and queen, who were astonished on seeing it. They summoned a pandit and asked him about it; the pandit said that this was a case of mansa karma having arisen. As for when that karma might be released, he explained that in that city an oilman's son had died, and mourning for him was to be observed; when the townspeople spoke against it, all the other faults of the daughter were then cleared away, but one mark of play and one fleck of indigo dye still appeared to her in her sleep, though they could not be seen once she woke. The pandit was then called again and asked about this remaining trace; he said, "In your city there lives a Vaishnav couple, husband and wife, both devoted, in loyal chastity, to God alone. You have not yet given credence to their standing, and that is why this remaining taint persists; summon them and have their darshan performed, and it will be cured." On hearing this, the king summoned that Vaishnav husband and wife, and through their darshan the karma was indeed removed. For this reason the Vaishnav Jivandasji said: "Brother! Among all forms of karma, mansa karma is the greatest, and it cannot be removed." -- A sakhi (couplet) follows:

_Kabir koti karam palmaa kare, e manko vishaya svaad, sadguru shabda maane nahi, to janam gamaayo baad. ||1||_ (Sadguru Kabirji says: this mind, in the very act of relishing sense-pleasures, commits millions of karmas in an instant. If you do not heed the sadguru's teaching to stay away from these sensual desires, then you squander your human birth in vain.)

Sadguru Kabirji says that this mind commits crores of karmas in a moment while enjoying the taste of sensory pleasures. If you do not heed the teaching the sadguru has given, to stay away from these sensual desires, then you squander your human birth uselessly.

_Kabir kaaya deval man dhvaja, vikhe lehar phaharaaye, man chalante tan chale, taako sarvas jaay. ||2||_ (Das Kabirji says: the body is a temple, and the mind is a flag atop it, fluttering in the breeze of sense-desire; but though the mind may run after sense-objects, if the body too follows suit, then everything one has is destroyed.)

Das Kabirji says that upon the temple that is the body, the flag that is the mind flutters in the wind of sensory desire. But even if the mind runs toward sense-objects, if the body too acts accordingly, then a man's entire wealth is destroyed.

_Kabir manke mate naa chaaliye, chhaandiye jeevki baani, traaku keraa taar jyu, dalti apootha aani. ||3||_ (Das Kabirji says: do not walk according to the mind's own wishes; give up the soul's habitual restlessness -- just as the thread a spinner spins on the wheel is, in the end, wound back onto the spindle, so too should the mind be turned inward and joined to the soul.)

Das Kabirji says that one should not walk according to the mind's own inclination. One should give up the restless nature -- as the spinner of thread, having spun the thread on the spinning wheel, winds it back onto the spindle, so too should the mind be turned inward and joined to the soul.

Shri Vaishnav Jivandasji said: if one has kept the soul under control, then this is the means by which mansa karma can be released -- the mind must be brought under one's control.

In the Samagam, the chapter on the departure to the eternal abode is the last chapter, but this chapter on the removal of women's taint is Jivanji Maharaj's final great work of revolutionary accomplishment. Hence this chapter on the removal of women's taint offers a vision of the pinnacle of revolutionary change that remained to be completed at the very end. But because the inquiring devotees' devotion keeps finding occasion to display Jivanji's teachings, the devout devotees who transcribed copies of the Samagam have, by referring to what Jivanji Maharaj showed us of the words of Padmanabh and Adhyaruji, made an addition to the transcribed copy of the Samagam.

That Samagam is the one of Dhanora-Puniyad -- that is, up to this point, whatever has been added to the transcribed copy of the Samagam was composed by Jivandasji Maharaj during his stay at Dhanero and Puniyad.

In that Samagam of Dhanora and Puniyad, the Vaishnav Jivandasji posed a question. What has been written down is the record of Shri Padmanabhji and of Adhyaruji.

In the year Samvat 1458, on the fifth of the bright half of Magh, on the day of Vasant Panchami, Shri Padmanabhji
